title: Does osteopathic treatment have an effect on persistent symptoms in women with Hashimoto's thyroiditis undergoing hormone replacement therapy?
summary: Thyroid dysfunction is among the most common endocrine disorders in the Western world. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (HT) is the most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism. The condition goes beyond mere hormonal insufficiency and is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events and certain thyroid malignancies. Standard treatment is lifelong levothyroxine (LT4) replacement therapy. In daily osteopathic practice, HT is frequently identified as a secondary diagnosis in many women; clinical observations suggest that osteopathic treatment leads to a positive change in persistent symptoms..

interventions.name: Patients in the intervention group receive 5 osteopathic treatments at intervals of approximately 14 days.
Patients in the control group will not receive any osteopathic treatment until the 10th week. After that, they will also receive 5 osteopathic treatments.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Medically confirmed diagnosis of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis according to ICD-10 code E06.3 (anti-TPO-positive and/or anti-Tg-positive, with compatible ultrasound findings), as evidenced by a medical certificate
- Stable levothyroxine therapy for at least 6 months (TSH within the reference range: 0.4–4.0 mlU/L)
- Persistent symptoms (e.g., fatigue, depressive mood, cognitive impairment) despite biochemically adequate LT4 therapy, ≥ 4 on the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS)
- Written informed consent
- Sufficient knowledge of the German language
Exclusion criteria:
a) Pregnancy or breastfeeding
b) Thyroid disorders other than hyperthyroidism (e.g., Graves’ disease, subacute thyroiditis)
c) Severe psychiatric disorders requiring treatment with psychotropic medications
d) Severe cardiovascular, oncological, or other systemic diseases that could jeopardize study participation
e) Ongoing immunosuppressive therapy
f) Substance abuse (alcohol, drugs, medications)
g) Osteopathic treatments within the last 12 months, provided they involved visceral or cranial issues
h) Participation in other studies
i) Unable to provide an email address
k) Lack of skills or ability to operate or use tablets or computers independently
